articles.headline: Bad Lands Live Stock Association.
articles.text:
At the meeting of the committee of five held last evening at THE COW BOY office for the purpose of drafting by-laws and other business to come up before the Bad Lands organization, all the members of the committee were present, consisting of Messrs. Barr, Paddock, Eaton, Merrifield and Packard. It is, of course, understood, that all the by-laws and general business proposed by the committee are subjected to approval, rejection or amendment by the association. The by-laws are founded upon those of the Wyoming association as they are as near perfect as possible.

Every cattle man in the Bad Lands should carefully consider every point made by the committee [and?] come to the meeting with his mind [made?] up as to how he shall vote.

The committee is enthusiastic over the prospect of a successful organization and every stock man in the Bad Lands should take the personal interest in the association which alone means complete success.

It will be noticed that the meeting for organization includes all stock men, whether owning cattle, horses, mules or sheep, and that it is to be held the third Monday in April. This date does not conflict with other meetings and gives plenty of time before the spring round-up. It was also the unanimous opinion of the committee that all classes of stock men should join the association.

The following is the list of by-laws and other matters to come up for consideration when the association is organized:

BY-LAWS.

SECTION 1. This association shall be known as the Bad Lands Live Stock Association.

SEC. 2. The object of this association is to advance the interests of the stock growers and dealers in live stock of all kinds within the Bad Lands, and for the protection of the same against frauds and swindlers, and to prevent the stealing, taking and driving away of horned cattle, sheep, horses and other stock from the rightful owners thereof.

ELECTION OF OFFICERS.

SEC. 3. The affairs of this association shall be conducted and managed by a president, vice-president, secretary, treasurer and an executive committee, consisting of five members.

All permanent officers of the association shall be ex-officio members of this committee.

These officers and above-named committee shall be elected at the annual meeting of each year and shall serve until tne annual meeting following their election, or until their successors have been elected.

Written proxies, approved as genuine by the executive committee, may be voted at elections.

The executive committee is empowered to fill any vacancy that may occur by death or otherwise in their own body or among the officers of this association and the person so appointed shall hold his office until the next regular election.

DUTY OF OFFICERS.

SEC. 4. The president shall preside at all meetings of the association. He shall see that all the laws and regulations thereof are faithfully executed and perform such other duties as may be required of him in these laws, as well as such as may be necessary to secure the objects and best interests of this association not herein otherwise provided for.

SEC. 5. The vice-president, in the absence of the president, shall perform the duties of the latter and if both be absent at any meeting a president pro tem. may be elected.

SEC. 6. The secretary shall keep accurate minutes of the transactions of this association. He shall keep a roll of members and a correct account of all moneys received and shall pay the same to the treasurer. He shall write and send all communications as directed by the association. He shall draw all orders on the treasurer when directed by the executive committee and shall make a full report of all the transactions of his office at each annual session. He shall deliver to his successor all books and papers and other property in his possession belonging to the association and shall perform such other duties as may be required by these laws and regulations or by the association. He is authorized to employ a collector at a reasonable rate of compensation at such time as he may deem necessary.

SEC. 7. The treasurer of this association shall receive all moneys belonging to the same from the secretary and pay the same out only on the order of the executive committee, attested by the secretary as hereinbefore provided. He shall keep a correct account of all such moneys received and paid out. He shall make a report at each annual meeting of the association and at such other times as the association may direct, of all the transactions of his office, producing therewith vouchers for all moneys paid out. He shall deliver all books, papers, moneys and other property in his possession, belonging to the association, to his successor in office and shall give bond to the association in such sum and with such sureties as may be required by motion or otherwise, conditioned that he will faithfully perform all acts and things required of him in this section.

SEC. 8. The executive committee shall meet immediately after their election and appoint a chairman and secretary. This committee shall have entire control of the inspectors and all the business of the association during its adjournment. It shall audit all accounts and order vouchers for their proper payments to be drawn by the secretary on the treasurer. They shall represent the association before the board of county commissioners and the legislature and in other similar positions during adjournments of the association.

At each annual meeting, this committee shall make a report to the association in regard to matters requiring their attention and shall recommend such measures as they deem necessary.

MEETINGS.

SEC. 9. The annual meetings of this association shall be held on the third Monday in April at 10 a. m., at the Little Missouri crossing of the N. P. R. R. Place to be selected by the executive committee and proper notice published.

Special meetings may be called at any time by the president, or in his absence, by the vice-president, and shall be called whenever requested by five members.

Eleven members shall constitute a quorum for business at all meetings.

The call for a special meeting shall state the object of such meeting and no other business shall be transacted at such meeting.

ORDER OF BUSINESS AT MEETINGS.

1. Calling the roll.
2. Reading minutes of last meeting.
3. Election of new members.
4. Unfinished business.
5. Reports of officers.
6. Election of officers.
7. Election of executive committee.
8. Election of brand inspection committee.
9. General business.

MEMBERSHIP.

SEC. 10. No person shall be a member of this association except a stock grower as defined by the executive committee. To become a member of this association, any person must be proposed at an annual meeting by a member, each proposition shall be accompanied by the fee for admission hereinafter stated and shall be referred to a committee of three members who may report immediately. A ballot shall then be taken on the application and three black balls shall reject.

All persons admitted members bind themselves and their employes to the observance of all by-laws and resolutions of the association that are now in force or that may hereafter be adopted, on a penalty of forfeiture of membership.

Membership shall be personal. No firm as such shall be admitted, but any number of partners may become members by election and payment of entrance fee in each case.

ENTRANCE FEE, DUES AND ASSESSMENTS.

SEC. 11. The admission fee shall be fifteen (15) dollars payable at time of election, and no one shall become a member without such payment.

The dues shall be ten (10) dollars, payable at the annual meeting for the year following.

Any member failing to pay his dues before the next annual meeting when the same became due, shall cease to be a member.

Any member who has been dropped for non-payment of dues, shall before he can be re-elected pay to the secretary all dues and assessments for the period from his last payment to the date of his new application, as though he had remained a member.

All members shall be subjected, not oftener than once per annum, to an assessment not exceeding one cent per head for all cattle, horses, mules and sheep of which each man may at that time be the owner and no resignation shall be accepted until all dues and assessments are paid.

The assessment may be levied in the discretion of the executive committee and shall be payable when called for. Failure to pay on or before the annual meeting following date of such assessment, shall work a forfeiture of membership.

The fund so produced shall be collected by the secretary and paid to the treasurer, and shall become a part of the common fund of the association subject to such regulations as before provided.

SEC. 12. Any member who shall divulge the proceedings of, or any action taken in any meeting of the association to any person or persons, or do any act calculated or that may injure or defeat any proceeding or action of this association or officers thereof, that may be instituted for the purpose of its protection or that of any of its members under the laws of this Territory, or of these rules and regulations, or that may be subversive of the interests generally of the association shall have a fair and impartial hearing at a special meeting called for that purpose, or at the annual meeting, and if found guilty by a majority of the members present shall be expelled.

SEC. 13. Any member of the association who shall be expelled therefrom as aforesaid, shall not again be received as a member thereof, and stock growers generally shall be notified of such expulsion.

SEC. 14. Whenever it shall come to the knowledge of any member of the association that any person or persons are engaged in stealing or killing stock of any kind, he shall immediately notify the executive committee of the association, who shall be empowered to act in such manner as will, if possible, bring such person or persons to justice and recover said property.

SEC. 15. These laws, regulations and resolutions shall not be annulled or amended except at an annual meeting, and then only by a vote of two-thirds of the members present.

SUBJECTS FOR CONSIDERATION.

Repeal of the herd law.
Bulls running with herd.
Setting off western tier of counties as a stock country.
Getting the trapping of beaver stopped so that there may be dams to hold the water.
Shutting up bulls between Feb. 1 and July 15.
Strychnine to be furnished for poisoning wolves and cayotes and bounty paid for their pelts.
That brand be adopted for all estray unbranded horses and cattle and also for unclaimed branded horses and cattle,
That no inferior stallions be allowed at large at any time.
Appointment of cattle inspector.

articles.text: There is a limit to all things and the limit to the cattle business in the Bad Lands will be reached in three years at the farthest. Although many good ranges still remain, the most of them have been taken. New men are constantly coming in, old cattle men are re-stocking and soon the Bad Lands will have its quota of cattle. This fact annihilates the only argument that can be brought against the fabulous profits of cattle raising. The territory which can be used for the raising of cattle is limited. The demand is practically unlimited and constantly increasing. It is utterly impossible that there shall ever be an over-supply. The only question for social economists is: If cattle are worth from $40 to $60 a head with fifty millions of people to supply, what will they be worth and where will the cattle be raised to supply a hundred million persons?
articles.summary: Editorial predicting the Bad Lands ranges will be fully stocked within three years and that cattle demand will outstrip supply.

articles.text: D. K. Wade's wife and daughters will soon arrive from Pittsburgh. Mr. Wade intends removing, upon their arrival, to Tepee bottom. It is confidently stated that Mr. Wade will be saved the trouble of grading a road to his new residence on account of the influx of visitors.
articles.summary: D. K. Wade's family will soon arrive from Pittsburgh; he will move to Tepee bottom.

articles.text: J. A. Beaumont is in town from his ranch. He reports that the deaths among the sheep have nearly ceased, and that the experience of this winter has taught such valuable lessons that success is assured for the future. He does not feel at all despondent over the prospect.
articles.summary: Sheep rancher J. A. Beaumont reported winter sheep losses have nearly ceased.

articles.text: The dance at the Pyramid Park hotel last Friday evening was an event in the social history of Little Missouri. Every one entered into the spirit of the good time and a thoroughly enjoyable evening was the result. The toilets of the ladies were noticeable features of the entertainment.
articles.summary: Report of a successful dance at the Pyramid Park hotel.

articles.text: We have received a catalogue of the Mayville stock farm, situated at Mayville, Dak. The farm contains a large number of pure-bred short-horn cattle, full-blood Cotswold sheep and Berkshire pigs. The opportunity is near at hand for our stockmen to buy good bulls at reasonable rates. Attention is called to the advertisement of the farm in another column.
articles.summary: Notice of the Mayville stock farm's catalogue of breeding stock.

articles.text: The funeral services of the infant daughter of Mr. and Mrs. Osterhaut, took place last Friday. The scene was one of the most affecting we have ever witnessed. The voice of the little son, repeating the words: "Don't cry, mamma," added to the grief of the parents, was enough to move the stoutest heart. After the funeral, a few friends of Mr. Osterhaut contributed a purse large enough to pay all expenses and erect a tombstone. It was a free-will offering that sprang from the friendship every one bears for the bereaved parents.
articles.summary: Funeral of the Osterhauts' infant daughter; friends paid expenses and a tombstone.

articles.headline: WE STILL "LARF."
articles.text:
The Pictorial Edition Containing the Rooster with the "Abbreviated Narrative"

Still Holds the Fort for the Freight-Route Is Ours,

The latest information settles the freight route question beyond all peradventure. Contracts have been made with the railroads for rates, with merchants for goods, and, alas, for the route that is "sunk in a gumbo slough," for the freight now at Dickinson, which will be shipped here and freighted to Deadwood from this point. Marquis de Mores has sent word from New York that a freight depot should be erected here immediately, not waiting either for his return or for the break in the weather. Six residence houses are also to be built at the same time.

The route from here is selected and needs almost no grading. It seems incredibly that such a good road exists right through the heart of the Bad Lands. We went out on it several miles, however, and with the exception of one little stream, which does not even need bridging, the road was as level as any street in a city. Of course, it is winding while in the Bad Lands, but except for this it is as good a road as can be found anywhere. We ask skeptics to not take any one's word for it, but go and be convinced for themselves.

It seems that John Cranston, the agent for the route, turned traitor and tried to sell out to the Pierre route. His scheme was nipped in the bud, however, and only the intervention of friends of Mr. Jones kept the latter from putting Cranston's skin in a very leaky condition with a six-shooter.

Mr. Roberts here has ordered all his stock to be in readiness to come in, and expects to start with full loads next week. Only one bridge is necessary and that will be built in a day or two.

Our citizens can now rest assured that in two weeks at the most the route will be in full operation. The first freight will consist partly of that which is now at Dickinson and there is plenty of bullion at Deadwood for the return trip.

A telegram was received this morning from Mr. Jones, dated at Deadwood, that the train should start from here as soon as possible.

On reading the last copy of The Dickidson Press we were surprised at either the inefficiency of the people who have the matter in hand there or the buncombe of The Press itself. Contrary to all our expectations, not a solitary thing has been done for the route from that place. In The Press account of the citizens' meeting the reports of two committees were heard. We quote:

"The committee appointed to confer with the Northern Pacific officials reported that the business entrusted to it had not yet been completed. The committee appointed to carry on correspondence with the boards of trade of St. Paul and Minneapolis reported that they had written to said boards of trade, but had as yet received no reply."

From previous issues of The Press we supposed that the road was decided upon and bridged in a great part at least. Again we quote:

"Under the head of new business, after some time spent arguing different points of interest, a motion that a committee of three be appointed to view the road and estimate the cost of constructing the necessary bridges on the route from this point south was appointed, consisting of John D, Barnes, L. W. Granteer and Wm. Walton. They will make the trip as soon as practicable, after which the work of bridging the streams will be commenced."

This needs no comment. The first thing they ought to have done was to see whether they had a good all-weather route. The Dickinson freight route then dwindles down to the bare fact that "as soon as practicable" the route will be "viewed." Oh, Scotty, thou hast given thyself away.

The Press in another article tries to prove that Dickinson will be the end of the freight route. But what are arguments compared to the hard, cold fact that "We've got there, Eli." A fair exchange is no robbery, Bro. Scott. You take the argument and we take the cake.
articles.summary: The Cow Boy claims the Black Hills freight route for Medora: rate and goods contracts are made, De Mores has ordered a freight depot and six houses built, Roberts will start freight teams next week, and the Dickinson Press is mocked for its rival route.

articles.headline: County Organization.
articles.text:
It seems almost incredible that there should be any opposition to organizing Billings county, but we know of two or three such cases. They are all either small or non-property holders, however, but lest their objections have some weight, it seems fitting that a few reasons should be advanced in favor of county organization.

In the first place, a failure to organize is an advertisement to the world that we are too poor to support a county organization. No one who knows this county and its capabilities would for an instant hold such a view, but to the prospective settler a lack of county organization would be prima facie evidence of its sterility.

As long as the county is unorganized we can do nothing toward bringing its advantages before the world. The greatest argument in favor of Billings county is the very fact of its becoming so rapidly settled in spite of itself.

The most potent reason for county organization, however, is that the laws may be applied by officers elected here at home. We are now under the jurisdiction of Morton county and when any case is to be tried or the application of the law in any way is wished for we must go to Mandan, one hundred and fifty-six miles east of us.

Take the case of a tenderfoot who comes here intending to go into the cattle business. He hears all sorts of lies about the desperate deeds of cow-boys and by the time he gets here is more than half inclined to turn around and go back. Suppose right on top of this he learns that the county is not organized, and that if any law is broken here, a telegram must call the sheriff from one hundred and sixty miles before the law-breaker can be arres[illegible] We have received, addressed to THE COW BOY, at least fifty letters from persons who think of coming here. At least a quarter of the writers wished to know about the county officers and whether they were well able to uphold the laws. The rest of the writers said nothing about it for the manifest reason that they thought the county was organized and the machinery running smoothly.

About the only reason urged against county organization is that the taxes will be so heavy. Of course, this reason has little or no weight with our best citizens as they know its falsity, those who do not know it we ask to consider for a moment the resources of Billings county. If all the rest of the world were shut off from us we could live as well as we do now, except for manufactured articles. We have as good agricultural, stock and mining land as there is on the face of the globe. There is no county in the United States that furnishes so many necessaries of life as does Billings. Consequently none can better afford organization.
articles.summary: Editorial urging the organization of Billings County, which is still attached to Morton County with court business in Mandan.

articles.headline: BELFIELD GOSSIP.
articles.text:
BELFIELD, Dak., March 12, 1884.

EDITOR COW BOY:

Quite an interest is being manifested here in the proposed public land legislation by congress relative to the reduction of public lands, within grants, from $2.50 to $1.25 per acre; also the bill permitting a four-months' absence during the winter. A petition has been circulated and unanimously signed by the settlers in this vicinity favoring the passage of said bills. It certainly is an unjust discrimination to the settler, who happens to locate within the land grant, to compel him to pay for land given to the railroad companies and no doubt has a tendency to deter immigration. The bill favoring a four-months' absence is of no less importance and confers a great benefit upon the holder by giving him an opportunity to occupy his time to better advantage.

Negotiations are being made for the establishment of a newspaper at this place. There is no reason why Belfield should be behind other cities in this respect, and with the hearty co-operation of its business men and citizens it will undoubtedly prove a very important acquisition in assisting to build up the town.

Wm. M. LeMoyne, of the Belfield Company, made us a short visit this week,

Jno. R. Thayer, who has been spending the winter in New York, has returned.

J. W. Harbison, our obliging postmaster, is confined to his room.

Robt. Montgomery, whom we reported last week as being on the sick list, is convalescent.

articles.text:
To our cattle men the fact is so well known that the Bad Lands furnish the best cattle country in the world that there is no need of mentioning the subject. To our outside readers, however, this may need proof. We ask, then, what are the prime requisites for a cattle country? The answer is as plain as the question, food, water and shelter. The best of food is rich, nutritious hay. It is here in the Bad Lands in greater abundance than anywhere else. There never has been and there never can be a snowstorm in the Bad Lands sufficient to cover the grass. On account of the broken nature of the country there are always bare spots affording excellent grazing to new cattle. The old cattle which know how to rustle will paw away a foot of snow to get at their feed and be as fat as a mole all winter. This standing hay cures so well that it is actually superior to that which is cut and stacked. We have seen cattle turn away from a stack of hay, apparently in disgust, and commence grazing on the dry grass.

The falsity of the idea that the alkali in the water is any detriment has long since been proven. It is, in fact, one of the greatest helps. Cattle actually refuse to touch salt when they have access to alkali water, and thus the ranchman is relieved of a large expense for salt. There is water in abundance, but the cattle in the winter can get along almost as well on snow. The herd of cattle owned by Mr. Lang, which we spoke of in our last issue as contending with so many difficulties, has not had a drop of water for over two months, and yet is as fat as any herd on the range.

For shelter, however, the Bad Lands is unsurpassed. The force of the wind coming over the buttes is greatly broken and a few steps at any time will take a person into a coolie where the wind is absolutely unfelt. The sun is shining almost all the time, and in the coolies during the coldest days it is perfectly comfortable.

There are now in the Bad Lands many cattle men who have had experience in every cattle country in the United States and who own from one thousand to fifty thousand head of cattle. We have questioned many of them and the invariable answer has been that nowhere in the United States is there a better cattle country than the Bad Lands.
articles.summary: Editorial arguing the Bad Lands are the best cattle country in the world for food, water and shelter, citing Mr. Lang's herd.

articles.text: An inspection of several herds of cattle in Lyons county, Kan., shows the prevalence of foot and mouth disease in its most terrible and deadly form. The report tells of animals still alive but slowly falling to pieces. It is difficult to understand why they should be suffered to live and spread the disease, instead of being killed at once. Strong measures should be taken, and that without delay, to quarantine the infected district and prevent a wider dissemination of the scourge.—[Pioneer-Press.
articles.summary: Clipped report of foot and mouth disease in Lyons County, Kansas.

articles.text: We have received a copy of the prospectus of the Keystone Cattle Co., of Glendive, Mont., which contains many valuable facts relative to the profits in cattle raising. The Keystone Company is a stock concern and there can be no doubt in the mind of a person who knows anything about cattle that money invested in the stock of such a company is bound to yield the largest returns.
articles.summary: Notice of the Keystone Cattle Co. prospectus.

articles.text: By the law of Dakota the following property is exempt from execution for debt. Homesteads, one acre if within a town plat, and 160 acres if not, with house and appurtenances, unlimited in value. Exemption is absolute except as to taxes, mechanics' lien for work on the homestead, and debts created for the purchase thereof. Personal property exempt, $150, besides wearing apparel, books to the amount of $100, provisions for one year, family pictures, etc. Real estate or personal property is liable for its purchase money, otherwise the exemptions are as above stated. Married women retain their real and personal property, and may make contracts, sue and be sued, as if single. Neither husband nor wife has any interest in the property of the other. Dower and courtesy are abolished.—[The Northwest.
articles.summary: Clipped summary of Dakota debt-exemption and married women's property law.

articles.text: The following buildings will be begun immediately: freight-house 100 by 32, six dwelling houses, restaurant, billiard hall and lodging house. Lumber is ordered, plans made and there is to be no delay whatever.
articles.summary: A freight-house, six dwellings, restaurant, billiard hall and lodging house are to be built at once.
